stem: A 23-year-old woman has come to the Infectious Diseases Clinic concerned that she may have contracted hepatitis B after risk-taking behaviour during a recent 3-month trip to Thailand. Her serology results are shown below. Investigations: Whcih of the following is most likely to represent the length of time this patient has been infected with hepatitis B? HBsAg Positive HBeAg Negative Anti-HBs Negative Anti-HBc Negative Anti-HBe Negative
explanation: She is only HBsAg positive, and HBsAg is the only serological marker detected during the first 3-5 weeks after being infected with hepatitis B.

stem: You are examining the pathophysiology of a degenerative neurological condition which is associated with cellular senescence in glial cells. Which of the following is associated with senescence?
explanation: Senescence is associated with cessation of mitosis, which is thought to be related to progressive shortening of telomere length due repeated cell division, with cell division stopping once telomeres fall below a critical length.

stem: An 18-year-old man presents to the Neurology Clinic with a bitemporal inferior quadrantanopia. Where is the most likely location of the lesion causing the visual field loss?
explanation: The pattern of visual field loss fits best with a suprasellar lesion, most likely due to a craniopharyngioma. Downward extension of the tumour leads to pressure on the upper portion of the optic chiasm first, leading to a bitemporal inferior quadrantanopia with smaller lesions, and as they extend a hemianopia.

stem: A 22-year-old man comes to the clinic for a routine appointment. He has undergone a splenectomy some three years earlier after a motor vehicle accident. He has been well apart from one episode of pneumonia in the past year. Which of the following is likely to be seen on the blood film?
explanation: Features of hyposplenism include Howell-Jolly bodies, Pappenheimer bodies, target cells and irregular contracted red blood cells. Risk of infection post splenectomy is at its highest in the first 2 years after splenectomy. Q.

stem: A52-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department by the police. He has been found outside the local secondary school shouting that he can protect the children from access to alcohol and drugs. He has dressed himself as a priest. Past medical history of note includes episodes of depression and drug use, and he has been taking fluoxetine for the last 4 weeks after splitting from his long-term partner. General physical examination and routine bloods are unremarkable. You note obvious pressure of speech and clang association while speaking to him. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The most likely diagnosis is an episode of mania related to the fluoxetine, which is likely to reach peak effect some 3-4 weeks after commencing therapy. The overinflated opinion of himself as a saviour of children fits well with the diagnosis. Withdrawal of fluoxetine and institution of a medication more appropriate for bipolar disease are appropriate. Q.

stem: An 80-year-old man presents to the Cardiology Clinic for review. He has been diagnosed with aortic stenosis but is currently not keen to proceed to surgery. Over the past 6 months he has developed persistent iron deficiency anaemia despite iron therapy, with a normal upper and lower Gl endoscopy. Most recently a capsule endoscopy has revealed evidence of small bowel angiodysplasia. Which of the following is the most likely cause of bleeding in this patient?
explanation: It is well recognised that shear stress leads to increased activity of von-Willebrand factor (VWF) metalloproteinase, and this is thought in aortic stenosis to lead to increased cleavage of VWF multimers. This in turn increases the risk of bleeding in patients with aortic stenosis and explains why iron deficiency anaemia often resolves after valve replacement.

stem: A59-year-old woman with a history of type 2 diabetes comes to the clinic for review.Current medication includes metformin and pioglitazone. She complains that she is continuing to put on weight, particularly around her hips, but is happy her glucose is well controlled. On examination her BP is 122/82mmHg, pulse is 67 bpm and regular. BMI is 32.Her weight has increased by 6 kg over the past 2 years. HbA1cis 52 mmol/mol. Which of the following most closely represents the mode of action of pioglitazone?
options: Increases insulin sensitivity in muscle and fat
explanation: Pioglitazone is a PPAR gamma agonist which primarily increases insulin sensitivity in muscle and fat.

stem: You are asked to review a 73-year-old woman prior to discharge from the Stroke Unit. She has recovered well but feels that she has some residual visual field loss. You examine her and identify a right superior quadrantanopia. Where is the likely site of the lesion?
explanation: This pattern of visual field loss suggests damage to the inferior optic radiation, on the opposite side to the deficit(in this case the left-hand side). This is most likely where it passes through the temporal lobe. Q.

stem: A36-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with acute onset severe reddening, pain and photophobia affecting her left eye. There is excess tearing and a left-sided frontal headache. Her only past medical history of note is ulcerative colitis, which is currently well controlled. Visual acuity is reduced and on slit lamp examination the anterior chamber appears hazy in appearance with cells in the chamber. The left pupil is more constricted than the right. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial intervention?
explanation: The clinical picture here with a red inflamed eye, coupled with a history of inflammatory bowel disease, is consistent with acute anterior uveitis. The initial intervention of choice is topical corticosteroids, coupled with cycloplegic agents that serve to reduce eye pain. Difficuty:Average.

stem: A 28-year-old soldier comes to the Emergency Department for review.He has suffered from a chronic cough and shortness of breath over the past 6 weeks and has not improved despite prescription of a salbutamol inhaler by his GP. Some 3 days earlier he had started erythromycin therapy for Mycoplasma pneumonia, but is failing to tolerate it due to symptoms of indigestion and diarrhoea. Which of the following is the most appropriate alternative?
explanation: Mycoplasma pneumonia generally responds to therapy with macrolides,fluoroquinolones and tetracyclines. As such, the most alternative option is doxycycline, where treatment should be continued for at least 7 and up to 14 days of treatment. Difficuty.

stem: A72-year-old man comes to the Ophthalmology Clinic for review. He has had difficulties with near field vision, loss of contrast sensitivity and adapting between light and dark. He says that when he goes out at night there is a patch of central visual loss which affects the visual field of his left eye, and during the daytime there is central visual distortion. Apart from hypertension he has no significant past medical history of note. Fundoscopy of the left eye reveals evidence of pigment deposition and small areas of reddening consistent with subretinal haemorrhage. Examination of the right eye only reveals evidence of pigment deposition. His BP is 152/94mmHg. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: Difficulty.

stem: A 42-year-old woman presents to the rheumatology clinic for review. She has undergone therapy for leukaemia over the past 2 years, including high-dose corticosteroids. She has pain in her right hip which started with groin pain on walking around 3-4 weeks earlier, and has now worsened to affect the right thigh and buttock. Examination reveals pain on hip flexion and internal and external rotation. Movement of the left hip is normal and there is no other sign of joint disease. Which of the following is the optimal way to confirm the underlying diagnosis?
explanation: The most likely diagnosis, given the history of previous leukaemia and high-dose corticosteroids, is one of avascular necrosis of the femoral head.MRl is reported to have 100% sensitivity for confirming the diagnosis, with a single density line on T1 images representing the separation of normal and ischaemic bone, and a second high-density line on T2-weighted images representing hypervascular granulation tissue Difficuty.

stem: A 64-year-old man comes to the Oncology Clinic for review. He has a left renal tumour and has been studying on the internet about the position of the kidney and structures which may be affected by the cancer. Which of the following is adjacent to the left kidney and not separated by visceral peritoneum?
explanation: The middle portion of the left kidney is adjacent to the pancreas and not separated by peritoneum. (see External Links).

stem: A58-year-old man presents to the Cardiology Clinic for review. He has cardiac failure as a result of previous viral cardiomyopathy and a recent ejection fraction on echocardiography is measured at 25%. He complains of persistent lethargy and shortness of breath on minimal exercise. Current medication includes lisinopril 20 mg, bisoprolol 10 mg, furosemide 40 mg. His blood pressure is 122/80 mmHg, heart rate is 64 bpm and regular and he has bilateral basal crackles on auscultation of the chest. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 120 g/l 135-175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 7.0×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 202×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium (Na+) 140 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.7 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 108 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Chest X-ray Cardiomegaly, prominent hilar vessels Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: The first angiotensin receptor blocker(ARB) combined with a neprilysin inhibitor, sacubitril valsartan, significantly improves symptoms and risk of cardiovascular death (a combined heart failure hospitalisation cardiovascular death combined endpoint). In the PARADIGM-HF study the endpoint was seen in 21.8% of patients treated with sacubitrilvalsartan versus 26.5% for enalapril. Here it is likely to impact on symptoms and risk of hospitalisation. stem: A70-year-old man with a history of cardiac failure comes to the Cardiology Clinic for review. He has suffered from decreased exercise tolerance over the past 5 months, despite therapy with ramipril, bisoprolol and furosemide. On examination his BP128/80 mmHg, pulse is 87 bpm and regular. There is a pan-systolic murmur loudest in the mitral area, and crackles at both lung bases on auscultation. There is minimal ankle swelling. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 119 g/l 135-175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 6.7×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 179×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 141 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/l Potassium(K+) 5.1 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 134μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Ejection fraction Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: This patient has a resting pulse rate above target of 75 BPM, and is in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. In this patient population control of heart rate with ivabradine has been proven in clinical trials to improve outcomes. The SHIFT study conducted in patients with stable chronic heart failure showed a reduction in a combined outcome of cardiovascular mortality and hospital admission for heart failure of 18% for patients prescribed ivabradine versus those prescribed placebo, on top of standard of care. Cardiac Failure Media explanations.

stem: A70-year-old man with a history of cardiac failure and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease comes to the Emergency Department complaining of palpitations. He takes a range of chronic medications, and has recently been started on clarithromycin by his GP for a respiratory tract infection. On examination his BP is 138/82mmHg, pulse is 78 bpm and regular. He has bilateral poor air entry, and crackles at the right lung base. Abdomen is soft and non-tender and, there is bilateral pitting oedema of the lower limbs. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 131 g/l 135-175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 11.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 207×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 140 mmol/l 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 5.0 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 122 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L ECG Sinus rhythm, QT interval 520 ms, ventricular rate 78 bpm Which of the following is the most likely cause of long QT in this patient?
explanation: Macrolides such as clarithromycin are well recognised as a cause of long QT syndrome, and clarithromycin is therefore the most likely cause of the ECG changes seen here. Withdrawal of medication is likely to result in a fall in the QT interval. QT prolongation increases the risk of torsades, which may account for the palpitations reported here. In addition to medication withdrawal, magnesium sulphate by intravenous infusion is the treatment of choice for torsades. Long QT Syndrome explanations.

According to her husband, she has suffered from worsening tiredness, dizziness and double vision over the past few days.You suspect she may be thiamine deficient. Which of the following is the most likely finding in this patient?
explanation: Given that women in pregnancy generally present early with health problems, it's most likely this patient.
