stem: A 55-year-old consultant physician presents to the Haematology Clinic with a diagnosis of acute myeloid leukaemia(AML). He asks about the likely outcome of his disease on the basis of current work-up findings. Which of the following features in his work-up would be associated with a good prognosis?
explanation: 60% is taken as the pivot point between good and poor outlook for AML,with scores greater than 60% indicating a better prognosis. It is a score of functional status.

stem: A72-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a severe headache, vomiting and drowsiness. He has a history of hypertension and continues to smoke 20 cigarettes per day. On examination his BP is 185/105mmHg,pulse is 85 bpm and regular. He is complaining of a severe headache and is mildly confused with a GCS of 13. There is a right homonymous hemianopia. An initial CT head scan is unremarkable. Where is the most likely interruption in blood flow?
explanation: The visual field loss here fits with loss of blood supply to the left occipital lobe, consistent with a posterior cerebral artery infarct.MRI scanning is optimal for identifying posterior territory infarction, and early changes are less likely to be apparent on CT scanning (as here).

stem: A52-year-old woman comes to the clinic for review. Her mother is 78 years old and has had a number of osteoporotic fractures. She is worried about her own risk of osteoporosis and has paid for a private DEXA scan. The results show a T score of 0.5 and a Z score of 0.1. Routine bloods including calcium are in the normal range. Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action for managing her osteoporosis risk?
explanation: The T score indicates a bone mineral density 5% above that expected for a woman in the 20-30 age group, indicating no increased risk of osteoporosis. The Z score also indicates a BMD very close to the expected age related mean. As such no treatment is indicated.

stem: An 18-year-old man is reviewed in the Cardiology Clinic after the sudden death of his father at the age of 42 years. You understand that one uncle has also died suddenly without any past medical history. He has no past medical history of note, although he does admit to having been light-headed after a run a few months earlier. On examination his BP is 118/82 mmHg, pulse is 62 bpm and regular. There are no heart murmurs and his chest is clear. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 137 g/l 135-175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 6.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 192×109/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 138 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 80 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L ECG Sinus rhythm,QTcF 510 ms 24-hour tape Frequent ventricular ectopics but nil else of note Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: The most likely diagnosis is congenital long QT syndrome,for which beta blockade iseffective in preventing episodes of symptomatic VTin 70% of patients. Atenolol, propranolol and metoprolol are all used as potential options.

stem: A 49-year-old homeless man is admitted to the Emergency Department having taken an overdose of amyl nitrate which was given to him by a passer-by. On examination in the Emergency Department he is cyanosed, has a respiratory rate of 30, and complains of severe shortness of breath with chest pain. His BP is 100/60 mmHg, pulse is 92 bpm and regular. You suspect methaemoglobinaemia. Which of the following is the pathophysiological process which underlies this?
options: Shunting due to increased nitrate levels
explanation: This is associated with greatly reduced affinity of blood cells to bind oxygen, leading to severe symptoms of tissue hypoxia. Exogenous sources of nitrate, a popular recreational drug, are well recognised as causes of methaemoglobinaemia. Methylene blue and ascorbic acid are potential interventions in the management of the condition.

stem: A 45-year-old woman with a diagnosis of Guillain-Barré syndrome(GBS) is reviewed on the ward. She has ascending weakness that has continued to progress despite a second course of IV immunoglobulin.You have been asked to see her because she complains of worsening shortness of breath, particularly if she lies flat. On examination her BP is 110/70 mmHg, pulse is 75 bpm and regular. She has 3/5 power weakness affecting both lower limbs and is unable to sit up properly in the bed without help. Her chest is clear. Which of the following is the most useful way to assess need for ITU care?
explanation: Forced vital capacity (FVC) is directly linked to outcomes in GBS, with respiratory failure the most common cause of death in association with GBS. An FVC reduction to less than 20 ml/kg is the usual indication for transfer to the ITU;a fall to below 15 ml/kg the usual criterion for intubation.

stem: A 62-year-old man presents to the Diabetes Clinic for review.Unfortunately, he suffered a large lower GI haemorrhage, thought to be related to diverticular disease, some 3 weeks earlier. He required a 4-unit blood transfusion. His blood glucose control on a combination of metformin and gliclazide is erratic. When is the optimal time to measure his HbA1c from his last packed cell transfusion?
explanation: Red cell lifespan is approximately 120 days.As such, after a significant blood transfusion, it is only of value to check HbA1c after an interval of at least 12 weeks. Checking it earlier than this time is likely to result in a falsely low result, driving inappropriate changes in blood glucose therapy.

stem: A 49-year-old woman comes to the Emergency Department complaining of an episode of fast palpitations which lasted for approximately 90 minutes. She says they were irregular in nature, and too fast to count. She also felt faint and had to lie down during the period of palpitations. On further questioning it transpires that other episodes have occurred approximately once per week over the past 4 months. On examination in the clinic her BP is 125/82 mmHg, pulse is 65 bpm and regular. Heart sounds are normal, her chest is clear, abdomen is soft and non-tender.12 lead ECG is normal, as is her chest X-ray. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: Q. Answered Flagged In this situation with regular infrequent palpitations, most likely due to paroxysmal AF(PAF), although the intermittent nature of the palpitations makes capture difficult. A modern ECG recorder which transmits the ECG by mobile phone, and can be used when palpitations occur, is, therefore, the most appropriate next step.

stem: A 25-year-old builder presents to the Emergency Department with sudden-onset right-sided pleuritic chest pain which came on while he was lifting a pile of bricks. He smokes five cigarettes per day and has no significant past medical illnesses. On examination his BP is 122/72 mmHg, his pulse is 88 bpm, he is complaining of pleuritic chest pain at rest. There is decreased air entry on the right hand side on auscultation. Chest X-ray reveals a right-sided pneumothorax with a 3 cm rim of air. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Admit for 4 hours for analgesia and observation
explanation: In this situation with a primary pneumothorax, even a rim of air2 cm can be aspirated in the first instance, as such a cannula is the most appropriate intervention. If this fails to reduce the area of air to below 2 cm or symptoms do not resolve, then chest drain is indicated.

stem: A 24-year-old woman is brought to the Emergency department by her husband. She has refused to leave the house for the past 6 weeks because she believes she is at imminent risk of catching bird flu. She tells you that this is going to happen because her husband has hung red and green socks up on the washing linein a particular order, and that she can hear a third person providing commentary on her actions. According to her husband she has become progressively more unkempt over the past 4 months, believing that she can catch disease from the water coming out of the bathroom taps. She refuses to comply with a physical examination. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Q. Answered Flagged The key to making the diagnosis here is the bizarre belief that she is at risk of bird flu,coupled with a delusion of reference (the hanging of socks on the washing line) and evidence of auditory hallucinations. The input of the multi-disciplinary psychiatric team is crucial with respect to management of the condition, and modern atypical anti-psychotics are the first-line intervention of choice.

stem: A 32-year-old man who is the captain of his work softball team comes to the Rheumatology Clinic for review. He has palpable tenderness over the medial epicondyle of his right elbow and there is pain on resisted elbow flexion. There is pain going down the arm with some numbness and tingling affecting the fourth and fifth fingers. Which of the following nerves is most likely to have been affected?
explanation: Ulnar nerve entrapment is seen in up to 20% of patients with medial epicondylitis, particularly sports people who work as golfers or pitchers in softball/baseball. It is characterised by abnormal sensation over the fourth and fifth fingers. It very rarely progresses to muscle wasting over the ulnar distribution because a diagnosis is made much earlier. Nerve conduction studies and electromyography are indicated to confirm the diagnosis and exclude other neuromuscular disorders.

stem: A 62-year-old man with a history of hypertension, diabetes and ischaemic heart disease, who is taking multiple medications including simvastatin 10 mg, aspirin 75 mg, lisinopril 20 mg, amlodipine 5mg and metformin 1 g, comes to the Emergency Department with a productive cough. He is diagnosed with a left lower lobe pneumonia that can be managed at home with oral antibiotics, and is discharged on clarithromycin because he is allergic to penicillin. Which of the following of his regular medications should be discontinued while on clarithromycin?
explanation: Simvastatin is metabolised by CYP3A4 and clarithromycin is a potent CYP3A4 inhibitor. There is a significant risk that when clarithromycin is co-prescribed with simvastatin, a steep rise in plasma levels of the statin may be seen, leading to myopathy or abnormal liver function tests. As such the simvastatin should be discontinued while the clarithromycin is being dosed.

stem: A45-year-old man presents with pain and swelling particularly affecting the fingers of both hands, and the toes of his left foot, which has increased over the past few months. Past history of note includes episodes of conjunctivitis and flaking skin on his scalp for which his GP prescribed a medicated shampoo.You note nail pitting affecting the nails of both hands and feet. There is distal interphalangeal joint arthritis affecting the right thumb and left middle finger, with significant swelling. Similar changes are seen on the left second and third toes. There is a patch of erythema over his right elbow. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 125 g/l 135-175 g/L White Cell Count (WCC) 6.5×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 187×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium (Na+) 140 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 100 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L C-Reactive Protein(CRP) 80 mg/l 0-10 mg/l Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Oligoarthritis predominantly affecting the distal interphalangeal joints with nail pitting fits best with a diagnosis of psoriatic arthritis. The patch of probable psoriasis over the right elbow and scalp also support this as the underlying cause of his joint symptoms.

stem: A72-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department after becoming confined to bed with severe heart failure and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. He has been unable to move in the bed and his wife is no longer able to cope with him. On examination his BP is 110/80 mmHg,pulse is 85 bpm and regular. He has bilateral crackles on wheeze on auscultation of the chest, and pitting oedema to both knees and over the sacrum. Which of the following scores is used to rate his risk of pressure sores?
explanation: The Waterlow scale and corresponding score card are used to estimate risk of pressure sores occurring. They are used to determine nursing care criteria and the type of mattress that might be used for the patient.

stem: A71-year-old man comes to the Surgical Oncology Clinic for review. He has had a squamous cell carcinoma of the bronchus diagnosed after presenting with a hilar mass on routine chest X-ray. He has smoked for 55 years and continues to smoke five cigarettes per day. Medication includes a salbutamol and a high-dose corticosteroid inhaler. He also takes ramipril, atorvastatin and aspirin after an inferior MI some 5 years ago. On examination his BP is 131/82 mmHg, pulse is 70 bpm, and he has atrial fibrillation. There is bilateral quiet wheeze consistent with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Which of the following is the biggest contraindication to pneumonectomy?
options: Two episodes of pneumonia over the past 2 years
explanation: In preoperative assessment, the FEV1 is measured post bronchodilator. An FEV1 of less than 2.0 litres is a contraindication to pneumonectomy, and a level of less than 1.5 litres a contraindication to lobectomy. If a patient's FEV1 is below these limits, surgery may still be possible, but more detailed evaluation is required.

stem: A 62-year-old man who has recently retired from his job as a solicitor is referred to the Haematology Clinic. He presents with night sweats, lethargy and anorexia which have increased over the past 4 months. He has no past medical history of note apart from essential hypertension which is treated with amlodipine. On examination his BP is 138/82 mmHg, pulse is 78 bpm and regular. He looks pale. You note marked splenomegaly and moderate hepatomegaly on abdominal palpation. Investigations: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 81 g/l 135-175 g/l White Cell Count(WCC) 28.2×10/(increased neutrophils, 4-11×10/L basophils and eosinophils) Platelets 442×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 139 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 5.2 mmol/l 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 132μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Alanine Aminotransferase(ALT) 62 IU/L 5-30 IU/L Alkaline phosphatase 134 IU/L 30-130 IU/L Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) 712 IU/L 100-190 IU/L Bilirubin 9μmol/L 2-17 μmol/L
explanation: The marked elevation in white count, which is predominantly of cells of granulocyte origin,fits best with a diagnosis of CML. The splenomegaly and elevation in LDH are other supportive features. Bone marrow examination is essential to determine staging and prognosis.

stem: A 22-year-old man comes to the Genetics Clinic for review. His father has just committed suicide at the age of 48,and it transpires that he had been diagnosed with Huntington's chorea but did not disclose this to his relatives. Physical examination is entirely normal. The patient has a number of questions about his condition. Which of the following would you tell him?
options: He has a 50% chance of inheriting the condition
He has a 25% chance of inheriting the condition
His symptoms are likely to come on at an older age than his father
No genetic screening test is available for the condition
There is a significant environmental component which drives onset of symptoms
explanation: Huntington's is an autosomal dominant condition characterised by trinucleotide repeat expansion of CAG repeats, which increase with successive generations affected by the disorder. Onset at younger age is seen in particular in South-American cohorts with the disease.

stem: A 28-year-old man who is 75 kg comes to the clinic for review to discuss how many calories he needs to eat to maintain his weight at current levels. He has a BMI of 23 and works as a solicitor.He runs three times per week each time for a period of 1 hour. His blood pressure is normal at 110/70 mmHg,pulse is 60 bpm and regular. What advice would you give him?
options: He should eat 1500 kilocalories per day
He should eat 2000 kilocalories per day
He should eat 2500 kilocalories per day
He should eat 3000 kilocalories per day
He should eat 3500 kilocalories per day
explanation: This is the recommended calorie intake for a male of average weight who follows guidance around maintaining regular exercise, who is not aiming to gain weight.

stem: A 65-year-old man comes to the psychiatry clinic with his wife. He has suffered from a number of episodes of bizarre behaviour over the past few months, including making sexual advances to a neighbour and laughing and swearing at a memorial service. On further questioning in the clinic it appears he has little insight into his behavioural issues, and he has recently been asked to leave his job as a solicitor because of problems with organisation and planning. Physical examination is unremarkable apart from noting that his hair is rather unkempt and he appears not to have washed for some time. His BP is 142/82, with pulse 70 and regular. BMl is 23. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The episodes of disinhibited and bizarre behaviour with lack of insight, coupled with problems with organisation and planning but without prominent memory loss, are typical features of early fronto-temporal dementia. SSRls may be useful in managing behavioural symptoms, and atypical anti-psychotics may have a role when there is severe agitation.

stem: A 29-year-old man who works in a printing business comes to the Emergency Department for review. He complains that he has lost the ability to distinguish between red and green colours, and this is hindering his job as a proof-reader. He was diagnosed with active pulmonary tuberculosis 6 months ago and has been receiving treatment with quadruple therapy. On examination he is apyrexial. He looks well with normal pulse and blood pressure. His chest is clear. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
explanation: Optic neuritis, which may be associated with loss of visual acuity, scotoma or colour blindness is a recognised side effect of ethambutol therapy that is dose-related but that can occur even with low doses in some, with a delay of at least 1 month after start of treatment. Ophthalmological surveillance is therefore indicated.

stem: A 29-year-old woman who works for an animal rescue shelter comes to the Emergency Department with mild fevers and lymphadenopathy affecting the left axilla. She has a number of scratches over her left hand and forearm, most of which are old that she attributes to a rescue of a litter of kittens from a derelict house some 2-3 weeks earlier. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
explanation: Bartonella henselae(BH) is the cause of cat scratch fever, symptoms of which include regional lymphadenopathy and fevers, occurring some 2-3 weeks after the initial inoculation. Kittens, particularly those with fleas, are a common source of BH infection. The infection is self-Limiting in most cases, although azithromycin or ciprofloxacin treatment may be considered for severe symptoms.

stem: A 48-year-old woman from the West Indies comes to the Dermatology Clinic for review. She has developed a raised rash on both shins which has appeared over the past few months, and she has had intermittent sweats at night. She smokes five cigarettes per day and has been prescribed a salbutamol inhaler by her GP for shortness of breath. On examination her BP is 152/90 mmHg, pulse is 65 bpm and regular. Chest is clear abdomen is soft and non-tender. You note a raised erythematous rash affecting both shins. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 121 g/l 115-155 g/l White Cell Count(WCC) 8.9×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 231×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 100 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Albumin 38 g/L 35-55 g/L Corrected Ca+ 2.82 mmol/L 2.20-2.60 mmol/L PEFR 470 V/min (485 predicted) Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This history of shortness of breath, coupled with erythema nodosum and hypercalcaemia in a patient of African Caribbean origin fits well with a diagnosis of sarcoidosis. A chest X-ray is likely to show hilar lymphadenopathy, and pulmonary function testing should be considered to rule out restrictive lung disease.

stem: A 19-year-old student presents to the university health service because of sudden-onset jaundice. He is currently suffering from a flu-like illness and has been off his food for the past few days. He tells you that he did have a previous episode of jaundice some 3 years ago, which resolved spontaneously. He does not report any symptoms of itching, has no past medical history of note, and does not use illicit drugs. On examination you note jaundiced sclerae. His BP is 105/82 mmHg, pulse is 82 bpm and regular. His temperature is 37.8°℃. There is evidence of pharyngitis. Abdomen is soft and non-tender, with no abnormal masses. Investigations: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 131 g/l 135-175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 5.9×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 210×10/L 150-400×10/L C-reactive protein (CRP) 52 mg/l 0-10 mg/l Sodium(Na+) 140 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 3.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 92 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Alanine aminotransferase(ALT) 15 IU/L 5-30 IU/L Alkaline phosphatase 85 IU/L 30-130 IU/L Bilirubin 43 μmol/L 2-17μmol/L
explanation: With isolated hyperbilirubinaemia in the absence of other abnormal LFTs, and an intercurrent illness, Gilbert's syndrome is considered as the most likely diagnosis. The C-reactive protein(CRP) is likely to be related to the influenza-like illness rather than to anything else. Gilbert's is autosomal recessive and occurs due to a defect in the gene that encodes for the conjugating enzyme uridine diphosphate glucuronosyltransferase 1A1(UGT1A1).

stem: A 20-year-old man comes to the Endocrine Clinic for review.He is concerned that he has not developed properly with respect to male sexual characteristics, and is finding it difficult to form relationships with women. He has no other past medical history of note. On examination his BP is 105/70 mmHg,pulse is 70 bpm and regular. He is 1.88m in height, and is slim with a BMI of 21.There is gynaecomastia, bilateral firm testes, and sparse pubic and axillary hair. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This patient is tall with gynaecomastia and bilateral small testes. The difficulty forming relationships raises questions around sexual function. Taken together with a normal sense of smell, these features suggest a diagnosis of Klinefelter's syndrome, due to an XXY karyotype.

stem: A 19-year-old man comes to the Emergency department complaining of joint pains affecting his left ankle and hip, right knee and forefoot. He also has conjunctivitis which has failed to respond to antibiotic drops given to him by the pharmacist, and pain on passing urine. He admits to having returned from a 'lads' holiday'to Spain some 10 days earlier. On examination his temperature is 37.7C, BP is 112/80mmHg,with pulse 75/min and regular. There is bilateral conjunctival injection, oligoarthritis and a psoriatic-type rash affecting both feet. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 130 g/l 135-175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 10.9×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 201×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium (Na+) 139 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 112μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate(ESR) 65 mm 0-10 mm in the 1st hour C-Reactive Protein (CRP) 112 mg/l 0-10 mg/l Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The suspicion here, with potential exposure to chlamydia, coupled with conjunctivitis, arthritis and keratoderma blennorrhagica, is that this patient has reactive arthritis (formerly known as Reiter syndrome). NSAIDs and antibiotics to treat any underlying sexually transmitted infection (STI) are the most appropriate intervention.

stem: A 54-year-old man presents to the respiratory clinic having been referred by the rheumatology service. He has increased shortness of breath over the past 6 months, and pulmonary function testing has demonstrated a progressive decline in FVC consistent with restrictive lung disease. He has been taking disease-modifying agents for the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis for the past 6 years. On examination his BP is 130/80mmHg, with pulse 70/min and regular. There is evidence of burned-out rheumatoid disease. Auscultation of the chest reveals scattered crackles but nil else of note. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 129 g/l 135-175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 7.9×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 189×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium (Na+) 140 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 112μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L C-Reactive Protein (CRP) 19 mg/l 0-10 mg/l Chest X-Ray Bilateral patchy shadowing Which of the following is the most likely cause of his respiratory symptoms?
explanation: Methotrexate is the standard first-Line disease modifying agent for the treatment of RA,and is associated with both pulmonary and hepatic fibrosis. Baseline CXR, respiratory and liver function testing is recommended before starting therapy, as is regular monitoring during treatment.

stem: A 19-year-old man presents to the Neurology Clinic for review. He has intermittent pins and needles affecting his hands and feet, which have increased over the past 6 months. He has suffered from a right Colles'fracture some 1 year earlier, and a lumbar vertebral fracture in the past 6 months, with a DEXA scan confirming osteoporosis. He also has abdominal pain and intermittent diarrhoea. He has a brother who has been affected by a similar disorder. Examination reveals a red-purple papular rash, eye examination shows corneal haziness, and you confirm loss of fine touch perception and proprioception in both feet. Which of the following enzymes is most likely to be deficient?
explanation: This picture, with an x-Linked disorder leading to a skin rash, osteoporosis, abdominal pain and neurological dysfunction, fits with Fabry's disease, related to alpha-galactosidase deficiency. Cells from skin biopsy samples can be shown to demonstrate alpha-galactosidase deficiency, confirming the diagnosis. Early detection of the disease allows for instigation of enzyme replacement therapy.

stem: A 64-year-old woman presents to the neurology clinic for review. She complains of persistent frontal headaches behind both eyes and affecting her temples, and feels she has central blind spots affecting both fields of vision. She has a history of hypertension and type 2 diabetes and has suffered a TIA some three years ago. On examination, her BP is 149/87mmHg,with pulse 70/min and regular. General neurological review is unremarkable, but fundoscopy reveals bilateral optic disc cupping, and visual field mapping does reveal bilateral arcuate scotomas. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Arcuate scotomas suggest a diagnosis of glaucoma, which fits well the headaches consistent with raised intra-ocular pressure and bilateral optic disc cupping.

stem: A 61-year-old patient has been switched from esomeprazole to omeprazole for the treatment of his peptic ulcer disease some 6 weeks ago. He tells you that his symptoms have been quiescent over the past 6 months since he started esomeprazole and he has experienced no deterioration since the switch in therapy. Which of the following is the difference between esomeprazole and omeprazole?
options: It is the R-isomer of omeprazole
It is the S-isomer of omeprazole
It is the calcium salt of omeprazole
It is the magnesium salt of omeprazole
It is the sodium salt of omeprazole
explanation: Omeprazole is a mix of the R-and S-isomers of the drug. The difference between esomeprazole and omeprazole is that esomeprazole contains only the S-isomer of the drug. Clinical trials suggest there is no difference between the pharmacodynamic effects of the two agents.

stem: A31-year-old woman with a history of Graves'disease attends the GP with her husband. He is deeply concerned as she washes her hands up to 15 times per day and refuses to sit down anywhere outside of her home or the family car because she is worried about catching MRSA. She opens doors when she is out by using her feet or waiting for others to come through them first. This problem started after she attended an outpatient appointment at her local hospital. Physical examination, apart from ocular signs consistent with Graves', is unremarkable. Which of the following best describes her problem with MRSA?
explanation: Her excessive hand washing and behaviour consistent with avoidance of her hands touching objects outside of the house is consistent with a diagnosis of obsessive-compulsive disorder. The most appropriate intervention is cognitive behavioural therapy potentially accompanied by a selective serotonin uptake inhibitor (SSRI).

stem: A71-year-old man with recurrent cellulitis comes to the Emergency Department for review after suffering a new episode affecting his left lower limb. A swab is taken for analysis and the Staphylococcal isolate is noted to be resistant to flucloxacillin. Which of the following is the cause of flucloxacillin resistance?
explanation: The primary action of penicillins is in disrupting bacterial cell wall structure through binding to penicillin- binding proteins. These can mutate, leading to decreased effectiveness of penicillins.

stem: A73-year-old woman comes to the rheumatology clinic for review. She has increasing pain and movement restriction affecting her left hip, and is now unable to mobilise more than a few steps around the house. She has a past medical history of asthma for which she takes salmeterol/fluticasone and salbutamol inhalers, a previous inferior myocardial infarction and hypertension. On examination both flexion and internal rotation of the left hip are severely impaired,although examination of the right hip is unremarkable. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 122 g/l 115-155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 7.0×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 302×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 144 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 100 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L C-Reactive Protein (CRP) 62 mg/l 0-10 mg/l Corrected Calcium (Ca+) 2.4 mmol/L 2.20-2.60 mmol/L Alkaline phosphatase 487 IU/L 30-130 IU/L Alanine Aminotransferase (ALT) 22 IU/L 5-30 IU/L Albumin 40 g/l 35-55 g/L X-ray bilateral hips and Joint destruction of left hip with joint space pelvis narrowing, bony sclerosis and hypertrophy of bone/overgrowth around the femoral head Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: The elevated alkaline phosphatase in the presence of a normal calcium, coupled with the hip joint changes seen, here fits with mono-articular Paget's disease. The intervention of choice here is bisphosphonate therapy which reduces bone turnover, significantly reduces pain and treatment can be monitored by any reduction in serum alkaline phosphatase.

stem: A 17-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department following an overdose of his mother's blood pressure tablets following a row with his girlfriend. He was found by his mother unconscious, with an empty bottle of vodka,and an empty bottle of atenolol 50 mg tablets at his side. On examination his BP is 78/50 mmHg, pulse is 34 bpm and regular. His GCS is 11 and he smells of alcohol. His blood sugar on finger prick testing is 4.3 mmol/L. His pulse and blood pressure do not respond to treatment with atropine 3 mg. Which of the following is the next appropriate intervention?
explanation: With significant bradycardia, hypotension and glucose in the low normal range, glucagon is the most appropriate next step. It increases heart rate directly via a cyclic AMP dependent mechanism and is a positive inotrope, driving improvement in both pulse and blood pressure. It is also likely to precipitate an increase in his blood sugar. High doses of glucagon are, however, required, and an infusion is often necessary. In patients who fail to respond to glucagon, external pacing is the next step.

stem: An 18-year-old comes to the Emergency Department complaining of joint pains, particularly affecting his knees and ankles, and a rash, particularly affecting the backs of his legs and his buttocks. He is particularly concerned because the areas of rash appear to be coalescing. On examination his BP is 115/82 mmHg, pulse is 68 bpm and regular. You confirm a macular rash affecting the backs of the legs and the buttocks, which appears to be joining together in areas of purpura. There is evidence of synovitis affecting his knees and ankles. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 134 g/l 135-175 g/l White Cell Count(WCC) 8.9×10/L 4-11×10/L Eosinophils 1.3×10/L 0-0.4×109/L Platelets 302×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 139 mmol/l 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 102μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Urine blood 2+ Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: The clinical picture here fits best with a diagnosis of Henoch-Schnlein purpura(HSP), which is a self- limiting condition in the majority of cases. As such analgesia and observation are all that is required. Only patients who develop hypertension or renal impairment may require intervention. The condition may recur and tends to present following respiratory tract infection.

stem: A52-year-old man who is HIV negative is diagnosed with Mycobacterium avium respiratory tract infection. He has a chronic cough and has lost 4 kg in weight over the past 2 months. On examination his temperature is 37.8℃, pulse 78 and regular, his BP is 140/80.There are coarse crackles at both lung bases. The abdomen is soft and non-tender with no palpable masses. Investigations: Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention? Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 121 g/l 135-175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 9.9×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 189×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 139 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 95 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Chest X-Ray Patchy shadowing at both lung bases CT thorax Nodular bronchiectasis
options: Daily dual therapy with ethambutol and rifampicin
Daily quadruple therapy with ethambutol, rifampicin, azithromycin and streptomycin
Daily triple therapy with ethambutol, rifampicin and azithromycin
Daily triple therapy with ethambutol, rifabutin and azithromycin
Weekly triple therapy with ethambutol, rifampicin and azithromycin
explanation: In this situation with significant bronchiectasis, daily triple therapy is the preferred option including rifampicin (preferred to rifabutin because of better tolerance). Treatment is usually continued for 15-18 months in total.

stem: An 18-year-old man is referred to the Gastroenterology Clinic with rectal bleeding. He also reports a sensation of incomplete emptying on occasions and vague abdominal pains. He has no past medical history of note and takes no regular medications. There is no family history of significant illness. On examination his BP is 118/82 mmHg, pulse is 70 bpm and regular. Chest is clear, abdomen is soft and non-tender,PR reveals an empty rectum. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 111 g/L 135-175 g/l White Cell Count(WCC) 6.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 191×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 140 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 3.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 100 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L C-Reactive Protein (CRP) 12 mg/l 0-10 mg/l Colonoscopy Multiple (100) adenomatous polyps Which of the following is the most likely genetic change?
explanation: The picture on colonoscopy is consistent with classical familial adenomatous polyposis(FAP), related to a mutation in the APCgene found on chromosome 5q21-q22.Patients commonly present in the second decade of life, and by the time they reach 50 years of age they may have up to 1000 polyps. Just because of the sheer number of adenomatous polyps, some can become cancerous and regular colonoscopy is required for screening.

stem: A 49-year-old man is reviewed on the recovery ward some 3 hours after a DC cardioversion for atrial fibrillation(AF). He presented with fast AF some 5 weeks earlier and was anticoagulated with warfarin. He plans to attend a wedding and drink alcohol in a few days'time, and wants to know how long he must continue his warfarin therapy for. A previous echocardiogram has shown no evidence of structural heart disease. For how long should warfarin be continued now he is sinus rhythm?
explanation: Evidence from observational studies supports continuing anticoagulation for 4 weeks after successful DC cardioversion. Longer periods of anticoagulation are not needed and increase the risk of bleeding; shorter periods may be associated with increased risk of embolic phenomena.

stem: A 26-year-old woman comes to the Gastroenterology Clinic for review. She has suffered from intermittent diarrhoea and lower abdominal pain over the past 6months, and claims that she has lost 5 kg in weight. She also complains of frequent mouth ulcers and had a lesion in the last 6months on her skin which was described by the dermatologist as pyoderma gangrenosum. Her only medication is the combined oral contraceptive pill. On examination her BP is 100/60 mmHg, pulse is 75 bpm and regular, abdomen is soft although there is some central abdominal tenderness, and PR is normal. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 99 g/L 115-155 g/l Mean Corpuscular Volume(MCV) 103 fl 76-98 fl White Cell Count (WCC) 8.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 381×10/L 150-400×10/L C-reactive protein(CRP) 59 mg/l 0-10 mg/l Sodium(Na+) 140 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 3.9 mmol/l 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 95μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Alanine aminotransferase(ALT) 24IU/L 5-30 IU/L Alkaline phosphatase 182 IU/L 30-130 IU/L Corrected Ca+ 2.1 mmol/L 2.20-2.60 mmol/L Albumin 30 g/l 35-55 g/l Which of the following is the most useful next investigation?
explanation: Faecal calprotectin is elevated in patients with inflammatory bowel disease(Crohn's or ulcerative colitis) and levels above 110 μg/g are considered abnormal. As such it is a useful initial non-invasive screening test for patients with suspected inflammatory bowel disease.

stem: A52-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with sudden onset weakness of both lower limbs and lower back pain. He has a history of hypertension and mild asthma but is otherwise well. On examination his BP is 142/82mmHg, with pulse 84/min and regular. There is bilateral increased tone with hyper-reflexia, and predominantly distal limb weakness. He has perianal numbness and has been incontinent of urine. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The predominant distal weakness with increased tone and hyper-reflexia, coupled with perianal numbness and early urinary incontinence, fits best with a diagnosis of conus medullaris syndrome.

stem: A51-year-old woman comes to the Haematology Clinic with worsening lethargy, night sweats and exercise intolerance over the past 6 months despite imatinib therapy that she has been taking for a number of years. Examination reveals that she is pale, with a BP of 105/80 mmHg, pulse is 90 bpm and regular. She has hepatosplenomegaly. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 89 g/L 115-155 g/l 21.2×10/ (increased myeloblasts, White Cell Count(WCC) basophils, eosinophils and neutrophils) 4-11×10/L Platelets 392×10/L 150-400×109/L Sodium(Na+) 140 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/l Potassium(K+) 5.0 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 121μmol/L 50-120 μmol/l You suspect imatinib resistance. Which of the following is the next appropriate intervention?
explanation: Dasatinib inhibits the activity of the BCR-ABL kinase and SRC family kinases along with a number of other selected oncogenic kinases including c-KIT, ephrin(EPH) receptor kinases and PDGFβ receptor. It has activity as a treatment for leukaemia both in patients who are sensitive toimatinib and in those who have developed imatinib resistance; it is therefore the preferred choice here.

stem: A 56-year-old man who is known to be an alcoholic and smokes 20 cigarettes per day, comes to the clinic for review. He reports suffering severe indigestion over the past 3 weeks and has now had two episodes of haematemesis over the course of the day. He undergoes an emergency endoscopy,and a bleeding gastric ulcer on the lesser curve of the stomach is identified. Which of the following supplies blood to the lesser curve of the stomach?
explanation: The lesser curve of the stomach is supplied by the left and right gastric arteries, the left gastric artery being a branch of the coeliac trunk.

stem: A39-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with sudden onset of a severe headache and pre-syncope. She admits to tiredness and lethargy over the past few weeks and a loss of libido, which is putting strain on the relationship with her husband. On examination, her BP is 105/75mmHg with a postural drop of 20 mmHg on standing. Her pulse is 85/min and regular. She looks pale. The chest is clear, the abdomen is soft and non-tender and her BMI is 21.She has a partial right third nerve palsy and bitemporal hemianopia. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 113 g/l 115-155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 7.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 179×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 127 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 5.0 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 112μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L 9 am:140-500 nmol/L Cortisol 85 nmol/L Midnight:50-300 nmol/l Glucose 5.1 mmol/L 3.5-5.5 mmol/L Which of the following is the most likely cause of her headache?
explanation: The hypotension, hyponatraemia and low cortisol reported here are in keeping with a diagnosis of pituitary apoplexy. It's likely that this has occurred because of haemorrhage into a pituitary adenoma. Diagnosis is with pituitary MRI, and assay of pituitary hormones is essential with respect to guiding replacement therapy.

stem: A34-year-old woman comes to the clinic for review. She has severe lethargy and depression and is finding it difficult to control her weight, having gained 8kg over the past 6months. She takes no regular medication. On examination her BP is 142/88mHg, with pulse 56/min and regular. Her BMI is 32. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 119 g/L 115-155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 6.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 181×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium (Na+) 134 mmol/ 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 100 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/l Low-Density Lipoproteins (LDL) 3.4 mmol/L 3.5 mmol/L Triglycerides(TG) 4.8 mmol/L 0-1.5 mmol/L High-density Lipoproteins(HDL) 0.8 mmol/L 1.0 mmol/L Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone (TSH) 12.2 μU/L 0.17-3.2μU/L Free T4 11.2 pmol/L 11-22 pmol/L Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: This patient almost certainly has subclinical hypothyroidism, as exemplified by the marked elevation in TSH and the T4 at the lower end of the normal range, coupled with marked weight gain and mixed hyperlipidaemia.The most appropriate intervention therefore is to initiate treatment with low-dose thyroxine.

stem: A73-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department with left loin pain and dysuria. She has had frequent urinary tract infections in the past, and this is her third course of antibiotics in the past 6 months. Other past medical history of note includes hypertension and mild asthma for which she takes a salbutamol inhaler. Her BP is 123/82 mmHg, pulse is 88 bpm and regular, temperature is 38.0℃.There is suprapubic and left loin tenderness on abdominal palpation. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 121 g/l 115-155 g/L White Cell Count (WCC) 14.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 201×109/L 150-400×109/L Sodium(Na+) 140 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.3 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 112 μmol/l 50-120 μmol/L Urine culture Proteus mirabilis USS renal tract and KUB Left staghorn calculus Which of the following is the calculus most likely to be composed of?
explanation: Proteus mirabilis is a urea-splitting organism, which can result in the formation of ammonium magnesium phosphate (struvite) renal stones, which can grow to extreme size when they are known as staghorn calculi.

stem: A 32-year-old woman with a history of severe asthma is reviewed in the respiratory clinic having been admitted for the third time to the intensive therapy unit over the past year. Current therapy includes high- dose inhaled corticosteroid and long-acting beta agonist therapy, monteleukast, and oral theophylline. She is unable to reduce her oral prednisolone below 10 mg without a significant increase in her symptoms. On examination her BP is 124/82mmHg, with pulse 65/min and regular. There is scattered wheeze on auscultation of the chest. Peak flow is 352L/min (520L/min predicted). Blood work-up reveals an elevated IgE, but is otherwise unremarkable, and chestX-ray is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: Omalizumab is a monoclonal antibody that targets eosinophils. It is indicated for use in patients with brittle asthma who fail to gain control despite maximal conventional therapy, where there is evidence of persistent allergy (raised IgE).

stem: A67-year-old man who has recently been diagnosed with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) comes to the respiratory clinic for review after an admission with pneumonia some 4 weeks earlier. He has a history of a previous inferior myocardial infarction(MI) some 7 years previously, when he gave up smoking (he has a 45 pack-year history). He continues to work part-time at the local supermarket and walks his dog some five times per week, although he says he's gained some weight over the past few months. On examination his BP is 132/82mmHg,with pulse 64/min and regular. There is some hyper-expansion on respiratory examination, although there is no significant wheeze. The abdomen is soft and non-tender and his BMI is 25. He asks about long-term prognosis. Which of the following is most important when determining this?
explanation: The BODE index is seen as the most effective way of assessing prognosis in COPD. It includes assessment of BMI, airway obstruction (as measured by FEV1), the distance walked in 6minutes, and assessment of dyspnoea using the MRC dyspnoea scale.

stem: A33-year-old woman presents with nausea, lethargy, night sweats and haemoptysis over the past few weeks. She has previously seen the GP on some four occasions in the past 6 months with symptoms of nasal congestion and nose bleeds, which she put down to a blow to the nose sustained playing squash. She takes no regular medication. On examination her BP is 155/70mmHg, with pulse 82/min and regular. There are inspiratory crackles on auscultation, and the pulse oximeter registers 92% on air. Abdomen is soft and non- tender. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 100 g/l 115-155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 11.9×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 187×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 141 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/l Potassium(K+) 5.4 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 198 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Urea 8.9 mmol/l 2.5-6.5 mmol/L Chest X-Ray Patchy shadowing Which of the following antibodies is most likely to prove positive?
explanation: The most likely diagnosis here is granulomatosis with polyangiitis(GPA). The history of sinusitis, most likely due to granuloma formation, is consistent with the diagnosis as is the evidence of pulmonary haemorrhage and abnormal renal function. C-ANCA is thought to be positive in up to 88% of patients with GPA.

stem: A34-year-old woman is admitted by paramedic ambulance from the airport having collapsed whilst departing a flight from Australia. She was reported to be complaining of chest pain and shortness of breath just prior to her collapse. On examination in the Emergency department her pulse is 94 and regular, and blood pressure is 80/60 mmHg despite administration of 1 litre of normal saline by the ambulance crew. The chest is clear although the respiratory rate is elevated at 28/min. O saturation is 90% on 60% O via a re- breather mask. The abdomen is soft and non-tender.You note a swollen right calf. She is confused and complaining of left-sided chest pain. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 130 g/L 115-155 g/l White Cell Count(WCC) 7.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 298×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 141 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 90 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L ECG S1Q3 T3 pattern suggestive of right ventricular strain Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: The most likely diagnosis here, given the symptoms of chest pain, low O saturation despite adequate O replacement, and ECG pattern suggestive of right ventricular strain, is a massive pulmonary embolism. Given haemodynamic instability despite fluid loading there is imminent risk of cardiac arrest,and IV thrombolysis is therefore the most appropriate next step.

stem: A72-year-old man comes to the Cardiology Clinic for review, saying that current medications are no longer sufficient to control his angina. He has taken atenolol 50 mg per day for the past 4 years,and has used PRN GTN until 3 months ago, when his GP converted this to isosorbide dinitrate given twice per day. He tells you that although he seems to get less angina, when he does his GTN is no longer effective. On examination his BP is 142/82 mmHg,pulse is 64 bpm and regular. His chest is clear. There is no ankle swelling. Which of the following is the likely reason that GTN no longer controls his symptoms?
explanation: Nitrate tolerance is a well-recognised phenomenon and is likely to have been manifest here by the lack of efficacy of GTN on top of regular nitrate dosing. Three mechanisms are proposed for nitrate tolerance, including impaired nitroglycerine bioconversion to nitric oxide, reduced bioavailability of nitric oxide and activation of the renin-angiotensin system as a counter-regulatory response to nitrate-induced vasodilation.

stem: A74-year-old woman presents with a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease(COPD) characterised by multiple admissions to the Emergency Department over the past 2 years with exacerbations. On this occasion she has been treated for the past 5 days with nebulisers, antibiotics and corticosteroids, and is noted to have persistent atrial fibrillation. On examination her BP is 132/82 mmHg, pulse is 88 bpm(atrial fibrillation). There is reduced chest expansion and poor air entry consistent with emphysema, and pitting oedema of both ankles. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 128 g/L 115-155 g/L White Cell Count (WCC) 10.9×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 189×109/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 140 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 5.1 mmol/l 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 105μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L ECG AF, rate 85, changes consistent with an old inferior MI ChestX-ray Hyperexpanded lung fields consistent with emphysema ECHO Bilateral atrial enlargement Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: Although many prescribers exercise caution when using bisoprolol in patients with a history of COPD, it is proven not to worsen symptoms of COPD. In the context of atrial fibrillation (AF) in patients with established IHD, it is effective in controlling ventricular rate and willimpact on overall mortality.

stem: A57-year-old man with a history of advanced alcoholic cirrhosis comes to the Emergency Department with increased abdominal swelling and tenderness. He has stopped drinking some three months earlier and maintains he has stuck to his regime of propranolol and spironolactone. He also reports fevers over the past 48 h. On examination his temperature is 37.9℃, BP is 105/80mHg and pulse is 92/min and regular. The chest is clear, the abdomen is soft but is generally tender and there is obvious ascites. There is pitting oedema of both ankles. He was admitted to hospital 3 times in last 5 months. Investigations: He is penicillin allergic, having suffered a previous episode of anaphylaxis. Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 100 g/L 135-175 g/l Mean Corpuscular Volume (MCV) 104 fl 76-98 fl White Cell Count (WCC) 13.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 75×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium (Na+) 134 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 5.1 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 90 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Albumin 24 g/l 35-55 g/L Alanine aminotransferase(ALT) 121 IU/L 5-30 IU/L Alkaline phosphatase 158 IU/L 30-130 IU/L Ascites tap 500 cells/mm Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: In a patient who is penicillin-allergic with likely spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, the appropriate intervention is quinolone and vancomycin dual therapy, usually oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg BD and weight- based vancomycin dosing. This covers post-Staphylococcus and a range of Gram-negative pathogens.

stem: A 28-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a headache, confusion and left-sided weakness. According to his partner he has been suffering from fevers, night sweats and decreased exercise tolerance over the past few weeks. She admits that they have been using IV heroin for some years. On examination he is pyrexial(38.4℃), BP is 122/60mmHg, pulse is 88/min and regular and he has an ejection systolic murmur on auscultation.You confirm the left-sided weakness affecting the face and arm. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 103 g/l 135-175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 13.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 112×10/L 150-400×10/l C-Reactive Protein (CRP) 232 mg/l 0-10 mg/l Sodium (Na+) 138 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.2 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 123 μmol/l 50-120 μmol/L ECG Right bundle branch block Which of the following investigations is most likely to help confirm the underlying diagnosis?
explanation: The most likely diagnosis here is left-sided endocarditis, potentially affecting the aortic valve, which has led to a septic embolus and presentation with the left-sided weakness. Although a CT head may be abnormal, it is only the echocardiogram that can confirm the source of the embolus.

stem: A72-year-old woman comes to the Dermatology Clinic for review. She has developed an extensive itchy rash with multiple bullae affecting her skin, but as yet sparing her buccal mucosa. She has a history of hypertension but is otherwise well. She has no significant symptoms of respiratory or abdominal pathology. Her only medication is amlodipine 5mg daily. On examination there is an extensive blistering rash with some intact bullae and some which have been de-roofed by scratching. You confirm that the oropharynx is spared. Which of the following is most likely to be found?
explanation: The presentation is consistent with a diagnosis of bullous pemphigoid, which is associated with antibodies to collagen type 17.Skin biopsy reveals IgG deposition on the roof of blisters, and C3 deposition is seen at the dermo-epidermal junction.

stem: 2 ):“ Lo 10cl.jxl A 44-year-old smoker presents to the Emergency Department with rapidly worsening health. He had an episode of influenza some 4 weeks earlier, and since then has suffered from increasing fevers, chest pain and, most recently over the past few days, haemoptysis. On examination his BP is 155/82, with pulse 85/min and regular. There are scattered crackles on auscultation of the chest, particularly at the lung bases, and respiratory rate is elevated at 24/min. The abdomen is soft and non-tender. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 91 g/lL 135-175 g/L White Cell Count (WCC) 14.8×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 197×109/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 140 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 5.8 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 198 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Urine Blood +++,protein + Erythrocyte sedimentation rate(ESR) 12 mm/h 0-10 mm in the 1st hour Chest X-Ray Patchy hilar and basal consolidation Which of the following blood tests is most likely to be positive?
explanation: The picture of rapidly deteriorating health post influenza in a male smoker, coupled with evidence of pulmonary haemorrhage and renal failure, with an absence of sinusitis symptoms, is suggestive of Goodpasture's syndrome. Anti-GBM antibodies are diagnostic of the condition, and plasma exchange is the most effective intervention.

stem: A70-year-old man with a previous history of peripheral vascular disease is referred to the clinic following a second episode of pulmonary oedema in the last 3 months. His GP is also concerned about a gradual rise in his serum creatinine. He has been treated for hypertension for over 12 years. On examination his BP is 155/90mmHg,with pulse 78 and regular.You note a left carotid bruit and no pulses below the popliteal bilaterally. His chest is clear. The abdomen is soft and non-tender, and there are no palpable masses. His BMI is 23. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 131 g/l 135-175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 7.7×10/L 4-11×109/L Platelets 299×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 140 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Bicarbonate(HCO) 22 mmol/L 24-30 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 3.6 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 182 μmol/L(up from 131 some 6 months ago) 50-120 μmol/L Chest X-Ray Cardiomegaly but no signs of failure Echocardiogram Ejection fraction 52% USS renal tract Right kidney 8.2 cm, left 11.5 cm Urine protein Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: With one small kidney and episodes of pulmonary oedema in the presence of a preserved ejection fraction, unilateral renal artery stenosis is the most likely diagnosis.The absence of other pointers to causes of renal impairment in the history, such as frequent UTls, drives us away from these alternative diagnoses. Medical management of hypertension is the mainstay of intervention for the condition, and there is little evidence to support more aggressive intervention with angioplasty.

stem: A 47-year-old woman with a history of primary biliary cirrhosis comes to the renal clinic for review. She complains of worsening bony pains and increased lethargy over the past few months. On examination her BP is 123/82mmHg, with pulse 73/min and regular. There are signs of chronic liver disease. Her abdomen is soft and non-tender with a palpable liver edge. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 109 g/l 115-155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 8.7×10/L 4-11×109/L Platelets 142×10/L 150-400×10/ Sodium (Na+) 140 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Bicarbonate 15 mmol/L 24-30 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 3.3 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 122 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Corrected Ca+ 2.1 mmol/L 2.20-2.60 mmol/L Alkaline phosphatase 203 IU/L 30-130 IU/L Plain abdominal film Bilateral nephrocalcinosis Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Renal tubular acidosis type 1 is associated with metabolic acidosis, osteomalacia and nephrocalcinosis, and therefore fits best with the clinical picture seen here. Autoimmune conditions including primary biliary cirrhosis are a recognised cause of RTA type 1.

stem: A72-year-old man comes to the respiratory clinic review after a second admission in the past 6 months with exacerbation of COPD. He is already treated with high-dose salmeterol fluticasone inhaler, and complains of persistent shortness of breath for which he is using a salbutamol inhaler every week. On examination his BP is 135/82mm/Hg, with pulse 65 beats per minute(AF). There is persistent bilateral wheeze on auscultation of the chest. Routine bloods are unremarkable. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: In this situation, where there is failure to gain control of symptoms on long-acting beta agonist and high- dose inhaled steroids, a long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LAMA) is the most appropriate next step. Guidelines recommend that LAMA is utilised irrespective of FEV1.

stem: A74-year-old woman presents to the Hypertension Clinic for review. She has been seen by her GP because of frequent headaches, and a 24h blood pressure recording has revealed an average systolic BP of 168 mmHg, with a diastolic BP of 82 mmHg. There are no signs of heart failure and her BMl is 23. Investigations: Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention? Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 120 g/l 115-155 g/l White Cell Count(WCC) 6.5×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 211×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 140 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 3.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.0.mmol/L Creatinine 95μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Chest X-Ray Normal heart size, no signs of fluid overload
explanation: NICE guidance recommends similar treatment for patients with isolated systolic hypertension as for those with elevated systolic and diastolic blood pressure. As such, given this patient is over 55 years of age, a calcium channel antagonist is the initial intervention of choice.

stem: A 50-year-old patient is prescribed granisetron for treatment of chemotherapy-associated nausea and vomiting. Where do you expect it to act?
explanation: Granisetron is a 5-HT receptor antagonist, which is thought to act in three sites: vagal nerve terminals in the Gl tract, chemoreceptor trigger zones located in the area postrema, and the nucleus tractus solitarius in the brainstem.

stem: A 67-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department with acute-on-chronic renal failure following a diarrhoeal illness. His creatinine has risen from 132 μmol/l to 327 μmol/L, and there has been a significant fall in his serum bicarbonate to 14mmol/L. He takes multiple medications for cardiovascular disease,peptic ulcer disease, epilepsy and diabetes. The PK of which of the following is likely to be most impacted by the renal impairment?
explanation: Warfarin is highly protein bound, and a significant change in acid base status driven by renal failure can markedly increase the unbound warfarin fraction. This in turn can drive a rapid increase in INR.For this reason in patients with renal impairment, INR should be closely monitored and warfarin dose reduced accordingly.

stem: A 24-year-old woman with a history of autoimmune hypothyroidism comes to the endocrine clinic for review. She is concerned as she has not had a menstrual period for 5 months, and reports decreased libido. Multiple pregnancy tests have proved negative. She takes 100 mcg of thyroxine per day and is compliant with therapy. On examination her BP is 122/82mmHg,with pulse 64/min and regular. Her BMI is 24. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 125g/L 115-155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 6.5×109/L 4-11×109/L Platelets 193×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 140 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 95μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone(TSH) 2.3 μU/L 0.17-3.2μU/L Follicle-Stimulating Hormone (FSH) 80 U/L 1-25 U/L Urine pregnancy test Negative Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Cessation of menses with negative pregnancy testing and a marked elevation of FSH, against a background of established autoimmune disease, suggest primary ovarian failure. Although the aetiology is unknown,it is more common in patients with a history of autoimmune pathology. No treatments are known to restore ovarian function, and hormone replacement therapy is advised.

stem: A 20-year-old man has presented to the Nephrology Clinic for review. He has recently been diagnosed with IgA nephropathy having suffered haematuria after a respiratory tract infection. On examination, his BP is 112/80mmHg, with pulse 72/min and regular. The abdomen is soft and non-tender with no masses. His BMI is 23. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 129 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 6.7×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 203×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 140 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 80 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Urine blood/protein +/- Auto-antibody screen Negative Which of the findings is associated with a more negative outcome in this situation? ABP 112/80mmHg
explanation: Small amounts of haematuria are associated with a worse prognosis in IgA nephropathy versus macroscopic haematuria. This may be because of later diagnosis, or a more prolonged disease course.

stem: A74-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency department following persistent vomiting and dehydration over the past few days. On at least one occasion these vomits have been coffee ground in nature. He admits to indigestion and intermittent vomiting stretching back over a year, although he has only lost a very modest amount of weight. He drinks no alcohol and is a non-smoker. On examination his BP is 105/72mmHg, with pulse 85/min and regular. There is marked epigastric tenderness. BMI is 23. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 105 g/l 135-175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 9.8×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 204×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 140 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 3.2 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Bicarbonate (HCO) 31 mmol/L 24-30 mmol/L Urea 12.9 mmol/L 2.5-6.5 mmol/L Creatinine 152μmol/L 50-120 μmol/l Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The history of chronic indigestion seen here, with only modest weight loss, coupled with anaemia, hypokalaemia, elevated bicarbonate and evidence of dehydration, is consistent with duodenal stenosis due to chronic ulceration with vomiting of stomach acid.

stem: A 72-year-old man is admitted with confusion and signs of a respiratory tract infection. He has apparently deteriorated significantly over the past few days with a cough productive of purulent sputum, lethargy and disorientation. He has a history of hypertension treated with lisinopril and amlodipine, and two episodes of depression in the past, but is otherwise well. On examination, his BP is 128/82mmHg, with pulse 80/min and regular.There are signs of right-sided consolidation. The abdomen is soft and non-tender. He is mildly confused, with a GCS of 14. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 129 g/l 135-175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 14.5×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 199×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium (Na+) 126 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 100 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Urea 5.8 mmol/L 2.5-6.5 mmol/L Chest X-Ray Right lower lobe consolidation Which of the following is the best way to manage his confusion?
explanation: This patient in all likelihood has a syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion (SIADH) as a result of his right lower lobe pneumonia.In the first instance, given the absence of significant neurological impairment,fluid restriction alone should be appropriate. There is no evidence of pre-renal impairment that would preclude this as a course of action.

stem: A72-year-old woman comes to the Rheumatology Clinic for review. She has suffered bilateral Colle's fractures and was diagnosed with osteoporosis following a DEXA scan which revealed a T score of-3.7.She is treated with denosumab. Which of the following represents the mode of action of denosumab?
explanation: RANK ligand promotes differentiation of pre-osteoclasts to osteoclasts, and upregulates osteoclast activity. Denosumab is a RANK ligand inhibitor which prevents osteoclast differentiation and is given as a subcutaneous injection every 6 months. It has the advantage over bisphosphonates that it does not accumulate in bone and does not carry the range of adverse effects of oral bisphosphonate therapy such as gastro-oesophageal reflux disease.

stem: A 23-year-old man comes to the Emergency Department with an erythematous, scaling,greasy rash affecting the skin folds around his nose, his ears, his scalp and his upper chest. He has recently returned from a year's backpacking in East Asia during which he admits to using illegal drugs including smoking heroin. On examination his BP is 105/70 mmHg,pulse is 75 bpm and regular. There is generalised lymphadenopathy and he has a BMI of 19.5. Which of the following is the most useful next investigation?
explanation: In a patient who has seborrhoeic dermatitis (the most likely diagnosis here) who has indulged in risk-taking behaviour, a diagnosis of HIV must be excluded. At some stage 85% or more of patients will have an episode of seborrhoeic dermatitis.

stem: A 19-year-old man is admitted to the Cardiology Ward having suffered a cardiac arrest while playing in an amateur football match. He was defibrillated at the ground using an automated machine, and the print-out reveals a diagnosis of ventricular tachycardia. He is conscious on admission to the ward and tells you that his father died suddenly of a suspected heart attack at the age of 42.Examination reveals a BP of 121/82 mmHg, pulse is 65 bpm and regular. Correct QT interval on the 12 lead ECG is revealed to be 510 ms. Which of the following ion channels is most likely to be defective?
explanation: Both LQT1 and LQT2, the commonest causes of congenital long QT syndrome, are associated with potassium channel defects. Together they make up approximately 90% of cases. LQT1 is caused by a defect in the IKs channel, and LQT2 by a defect in the IKr channel.
